---
title: "k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN)"
body-classes: fam-linear
---

[**Linear family**]{.fam-badge} · the simplest possible supervised baseline — it stores the training set and classifies a new point by looking at who its neighbors are. Grouped here with the baseline supervised methods, but unlike the rest of the family it is **non-parametric**: it assumes no functional form at all. Siblings: [Logistic Regression](logistic.qmd) and [LDA](lda.qmd) (parametric linear boundaries), [Decision Trees](decision_trees.qmd) (non-parametric, axis-aligned), [OLS](ols.qmd) (the parametric regressor it is most often contrasted with).

## 1. Essence

k-Nearest Neighbors classifies a new point by a vote of its closest training examples: measure the distance from the query to every training point, keep the **K** nearest, and assign the label that the majority of those K hold (Lecture 2, slide 8/10). There is no "model" in the usual sense — nothing is fitted, no coefficients are estimated. The training set *is* the model; "fitting" just stores it. All the work happens at **prediction** time, when the distances are computed.

It is the textbook **non-parametric** method: it commits to no functional form and has no fixed number of parameters — the effective complexity grows with the data (Lecture 2, slide 9/10). That makes it flexible (it can carve out arbitrarily wiggly decision boundaries) and almost assumption-free, but also hungry for data, expensive to query, and exquisitely sensitive to two choices: **how many neighbors** to consult (K) and **how distance is measured** (the metric, and therefore the scale of the features).

The single knob, K, *is* the [bias–variance](bias_variance.qmd) dial made tangible. K too small → the boundary chases individual points → **overfit, high variance**. K too large → the vote washes out local structure toward the global majority → **underfit, high bias** (Lecture 2, slide 8/10). The course's prescription is to **choose K by cross-validation** (Lecture 2, slide 8/10).

Compared with its nearest neighbors: [OLS](ols.qmd) and [logistic regression](logistic.qmd) fix a form (a line/plane) and spend training time estimating a handful of coefficients, then predict instantly; kNN inverts that — instant "training," expensive prediction, and a boundary that is local rather than global. [Decision trees](decision_trees.qmd) are the other non-parametric baseline, but they partition the space with axis-aligned cuts and ignore feature scale, whereas kNN measures raw distance and so *demands* that features be scaled.

## 2. When to use / when *not* to use

::: {.callout-intuition}
**Reach for kNN when…**

- You want a **fast-to-stand-up, assumption-free baseline** for **classification** (it also does regression by averaging neighbors, Lecture 2 slide 8/10, but the course uses it as a classifier). It is the "first model" you try alongside [Naive Bayes](../drill/exercise_02_spam_naive_bayes.qmd) (Lecture 2, slide 8/10).
- The **decision boundary is irregular** but locally smooth — kNN follows curvature that [OLS](ols.qmd)/[logistic](logistic.qmd) cannot, without you specifying any form.
- You have **enough data relative to the number of features**, and you can **scale** the features so distance is meaningful.
- You want intuition you can *point at*: a prediction is literally "these K labeled examples nearby."
:::

::: {.callout-pitfall}
**Reach for something else when…**

- **The feature space is high-dimensional** → the *curse of dimensionality* makes "nearest" almost meaningless (all points become roughly equidistant). Use a parametric model ([logistic](logistic.qmd)/[LDA](lda.qmd)), reduce dimensions first with [PCA](pca.qmd), or use a [tree](decision_trees.qmd)/[random forest](random_forests.qmd) that selects features.
- **You need an interpretable global rule** ("+1 unit of X ⇒ +β") → kNN gives no coefficients; reach for [OLS](ols.qmd)/[logistic](logistic.qmd), or a [decision tree](decision_trees.qmd) for if-then rules.
- **Prediction must be cheap or the dataset is large** → every query scans (a structure over) the whole training set; a fitted [logistic](logistic.qmd) or [tree](decision_trees.qmd) predicts in constant time (Lecture 2, slide 8/10: "computationally expensive for large data").
- **Features are on wildly different scales and you can't scale them** → the largest-range feature silently dominates the distance (see §3 and the wine example in §4).
- **The boundary really is linear** → a parametric linear model will match kNN with far less data and a readable boundary; this is the parametric-vs-non-parametric trade-off (Lecture 2, slide 9/10).
:::

## 3. Code idiom

The course teaches kNN both **from scratch** (so the distance-and-vote mechanics are not a black box) and via `scikit-learn`'s `KNeighborsClassifier`. Both run on the **same** iris split with **K = 3** and agree (§4).

**Canonical (sklearn)** — *(notebook `03_Supervised_learning_with_kNN (1).ipynb`, cell 12)*

```python
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

# Create a k-NN classifier with 3 neighbors
knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=3)   # n_neighbors = K, the only knob you must set
knn.fit(X_train, y_train)                     # "fit" just stores the training data
y_pred = knn.predict(X_test)                  # the work happens here, at predict time
knn.score(X_test, y_test)                     # mean accuracy on the test set
```

`n_neighbors` (the K of the algorithm) is the hyperparameter you tune — by [cross-validation](cv_info_criteria.qmd), per Lecture 2 slide 8/10. Everything else in the notebook is left at the sklearn `default`: `weights='uniform'` (every neighbor votes equally — `'distance'` would weight closer points more), and `metric='minkowski'` with `p=2`, which **is** Euclidean distance — exactly the metric the course defines (notebook cell 3).

**From scratch — distance, sort, vote** *(notebook `03_Supervised_learning_with_kNN (1).ipynb`, cell 7)*. This is the whole algorithm in three small functions, and shows literally what `predict` does under the hood — compute every distance, take the K smallest, majority-vote:

```python
import numpy as np

def euclidean_distance(x, y):
    """Calculate the euclidean distance between two points"""
    return np.sqrt(np.sum((x - y)**2))

def predict(X_train, y_train, X_test, k):
    """Find the k nearest neighbors of x_test in X_train"""
    distances = [euclidean_distance(X_test, x) for x in X_train]  # distance to every train point
    k_nearest = np.argsort(distances)[:k]                          # indices of the K smallest
    return y_train[k_nearest]                                      # their labels

def predict_label(X_train, y_train, X_test, k):
    """Find the most common label among the k nearest neighbors of X_test in X_train"""
    return np.bincount(predict(X_train, y_train, X_test, k)).argmax()  # majority vote
```

Used across the whole test set with **k = 3** *(cell 8)*:

```python
y_pred = [predict_label(X_train, y_train, x, 3) for x in X_test]
accuracy = np.mean(y_pred == y_test)
```

::: {.callout-pitfall}
**Scaling is not optional for kNN.** Distance treats every feature in its raw units, so a feature with a large numeric range dominates the vote regardless of how informative it is. The course notebook feeds **unscaled** iris features straight in (cell 4 — no `StandardScaler`), which is fine *only because iris's four features share a comparable scale (all cm)*. On a dataset with mismatched ranges it silently breaks: on `wine`, `proline` (std ≈ 314) swamps features with std ≈ 0.12, and raw-feature kNN scores **68.89%** versus **97.78%** once standardized (§4, computed). Wrap kNN in a `Pipeline([StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(...)])`. (`bincount` in the from-scratch version also assumes **non-negative integer labels** — fine for iris targets {0,1,2}, but it would break on string labels.)
:::

## 4. Worked examples

### Example 1 — iris, from scratch vs sklearn (the cross-check) {#sec-knn-iris}

The course's anchor example loads iris, splits 80/20, and runs kNN both ways on the *same* split so the two implementations can be checked against each other *(notebook `03_Supervised_learning_with_kNN (1).ipynb`, cells 4, 8, 12)*:

```python
from sklearn import datasets
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

iris = datasets.load_iris()
X, y = iris.data, iris.target                       # 150 × 4 features, 3 species
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=10)          # 120 train, 30 test
```

With **K = 3** on this fixed split (`random_state=10`), the from-scratch classifier and `KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=3)` both score **96.67% on the 30-point test set** (29/30 correct) — they agree exactly, which is the point of the cross-check (computed; the notebook stores no outputs for cells 8/12). The single test point inspected first (cell 7) has true label `1` and is predicted `1` (computed). Iris is nearly linearly separable, so even this minimal classifier with no scaling does well.

### Example 2 — choosing K is choosing your place on the bias–variance dial {#sec-knn-kchoice}

Sweeping K on the same iris split makes the [bias–variance](bias_variance.qmd) trade-off concrete (computed, `random_state=10`):

| K | train accuracy | test accuracy |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 100.00% | 96.67% |
| 3 | 96.67% | 96.67% |
| 11 | 97.50% | 100.00% |
| 50 | 93.33% | 93.33% |
| 100 | 75.83% | 60.00% |

At **K = 1** the training accuracy is a perfect 100% — every point is its own nearest neighbor — the textbook signature of **high variance** (it has memorized the training set). As K grows, the vote averages over a wider neighborhood; by **K = 100** (out of only 120 training points) the model is essentially predicting the global majority class and collapses to **60% on test** — textbook **high bias / underfit** (Lecture 2, slide 8/10). The sweet spot is in between, and you don't read it off the test set — you pick it by [cross-validation](cv_info_criteria.qmd) on the *training* data (5-fold CV here is flat at ≈ 94% for K = 3…25, computed; iris is too easy to produce a sharp optimum). The principle generalizes: **small K overfits, large K underfits, choose K by CV** (Lecture 2, slide 8/10).

### Example 3 — why scaling decides the outcome (wine) {#sec-knn-scaling}

To show the scaling pitfall from §3 with numbers, take `wine` (13 chemical features on very different scales) with a 75/25 split (`random_state=1`), K = 3 (computed):

```python
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

raw    = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=3).fit(Xtr, ytr).score(Xte, yte)        # 0.6889
scaled = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=3)
                       ).fit(Xtr, ytr).score(Xte, yte)                            # 0.9778
```

Raw-feature kNN gets **68.89%**; standardizing first lifts it to **97.78%** — a 29-point jump from one preprocessing line. The reason is mechanical: `proline` ranges in the hundreds-to-thousands (std ≈ 314) while other features sit near std ≈ 0.12, so before scaling the Euclidean distance is *almost entirely* the proline difference and the other twelve features barely vote. This is exactly why the Spring-2025 exam's Assignment 4 explicitly asks you to "scale if necessary" and notes that "distance/gradient models like k-NN" need it, while trees do not (§7).

## 5. Visualization

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: fig-knn-vote
//| fig-cap: "kNN classifies the red star (test point) by majority vote of its K=3 nearest neighbors (ringed), on three deterministic 2-D blobs. The dashed segments are the distances kNN ranks; the star is colored by the winning class. Reload to draw a new test point: where it lands among the blobs decides the vote — near a boundary the K=3 ring can straddle two colors, which is exactly where the choice of K matters most."
famLinear = (getComputedStyle(document.documentElement).getPropertyValue('--family-linear').trim() || "#2E86AB")
classColors = ["#2E86AB", "#06A77D", "#F18F01"]   // 3 blob classes
knnData = {
  function mulberry32(a){return function(){a|=0;a=a+0x6D2B79F5|0;let t=Math.imul(a^a>>>15,1|a);t=t+Math.imul(t^t>>>7,61|t)^t;return ((t^t>>>14)>>>0)/4294967296}}
  const r = mulberry32(0);   // deterministic; mirrors the notebook's np.random.seed(0) make_blobs idea
  const gauss = () => { let u=0,v=0; while(!u)u=r(); while(!v)v=r(); return Math.sqrt(-2*Math.log(u))*Math.cos(2*Math.PI*v); };
  const centers = [[-3,-2],[3,-1],[0,4]];   // 3 well-separated blob centers
  const pts = [];
  centers.forEach((c, cls) => {
    for (let i=0;i<26;i++) pts.push({x: c[0]+1.0*gauss(), y: c[1]+1.0*gauss(), cls});
  });
  return pts;
}
knnTest = {
  const xs = knnData.map(d=>d.x), ys = knnData.map(d=>d.y);
  const [xmin,xmax] = [Math.min(...xs), Math.max(...xs)];
  const [ymin,ymax] = [Math.min(...ys), Math.max(...ys)];
  function mulberry32(a){return function(){a|=0;a=a+0x6D2B79F5|0;let t=Math.imul(a^a>>>15,1|a);t=t+Math.imul(t^t>>>7,61|t)^t;return ((t^t>>>14)>>>0)/4294967296}}
  const r = mulberry32((Date.now() & 1023));   // new point on reload
  return {x: xmin + r()*(xmax-xmin), y: ymin + r()*(ymax-ymin)};
}
knnVote = {
  const K = 3;
  const withDist = knnData.map((d,i) => ({...d, i, dist: Math.hypot(d.x-knnTest.x, d.y-knnTest.y)}));
  const nearest = withDist.slice().sort((a,b)=>a.dist-b.dist).slice(0, K);
  const counts = [0,0,0];
  nearest.forEach(d => counts[d.cls]++);
  const winner = counts.indexOf(Math.max(...counts));
  return {nearest, winner};
}
Plot.plot({
  height: 340, marginLeft: 50, grid: true,
  x: {label: "Feature 1"}, y: {label: "Feature 2"},
  marks: [
    Plot.dot(knnData, {x: "x", y: "y", fill: d => classColors[d.cls], fillOpacity: 0.55, r: 4}),
    Plot.link(knnVote.nearest, {x1: knnTest.x, y1: knnTest.y, x2: "x", y2: "y", stroke: "#888", strokeDasharray: "3,3"}),
    Plot.dot(knnVote.nearest, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "#111", strokeWidth: 1.6, r: 9, fill: "none"}),
    Plot.dot([knnTest], {x: "x", y: "y", fill: classColors[knnVote.winner], stroke: famLinear, strokeWidth: 2, symbol: "star", r: 11})
  ]
})
```

This is the picture that earns its place for kNN: it makes the *algorithm itself* visible. The dashed segments are the very distances kNN computes and ranks; the three ringed points are the vote; the star takes their majority color. It also shows why K matters — drop the test point near a blob boundary and the K = 3 ring straddles two colors, the regime where small K is jumpy (high variance) and a larger K would steady the vote. This mirrors the notebook's own visualization idiom (a starred test point with its nearest neighbors highlighted on `make_blobs` data, cell 10), rebuilt with deterministic in-browser data so it needs no network or stored dataset.

## 6. Diagnostics & interpretation

What to look at to decide whether a kNN model is working:

- **Accuracy on a held-out set, and beyond accuracy** — report **precision, recall, F1** when classes are imbalanced (the Spring-2025 exam insists on this for Assignment 4, §7). A confusion matrix shows *which* classes the neighbors confuse.
- **The K curve (train vs CV accuracy across K)** — the diagnostic that locates your bias–variance position (Example 2). A huge train–CV gap at small K signals variance; both sagging at large K signals bias. Pick K at the CV peak, never on the test set.
- **Did you scale?** — the first thing to check on any disappointing kNN result. An unscaled distance-based model is the most common silent failure (Example 3): inspect feature ranges/standard deviations.
- **Dimensionality** — as features multiply, "nearest" loses meaning (the curse of dimensionality, §8 Mode B). If accuracy degrades as you add features, that is the symptom; reduce with [PCA](pca.qmd) or switch to a feature-selecting model.
- **Predict-time cost** — there are no coefficients to read; a kNN "explanation" is the neighbor set itself. Watch query latency on large training sets (Lecture 2, slide 8/10).

::: {.callout-bigpicture}
Comparative diagnostic vs a sibling: [logistic regression](logistic.qmd) hands you **coefficients** — a single global, interpretable boundary you can write down and reason about ("the odds rise with X"). kNN hands you **a local vote** — no global rule, but a boundary that bends to the data wherever it needs to. This is the parametric-vs-non-parametric trade (Lecture 2, slide 9/10): the logistic model generalizes from a fixed form and few parameters; kNN's complexity grows with the data and lives entirely in K and the metric. Match the choice to the question — interpretable global effect, or flexible local fit.
:::

## 7. Past-exam lens

::: {.callout-exam}
**How kNN shows up.** In the **Spring-2025 take-home, Assignment 4** ("Predictive classification challenge" on `SimulatedData.csv`, exercises 4.1–4.9, `phase0/exam_spring2025_notebook.md`), kNN is named as a **candidate classifier**. Two exercises bear on it directly: **4.3** asks you to "encode categoricals, scale if necessary" and explicitly notes that "trees may not need scaling; distance/gradient models like k-NN or logistic regression do" — so if you submit kNN, the scaling decision from §3/§4 is being graded. **4.4** asks for at least two classifiers (a simple baseline plus a more complex model) with justification, **4.5** for **hyperparameter tuning via CV** (for kNN that is choosing K, §2/§4), and **4.6** for accuracy/precision/recall/F1. Crucially, **4.8** is run by the grader on a **hidden hold-out test set**, so your preprocessing (the scaler!) must be wired into a pipeline that generalizes to unseen rows — a raw, unscaled kNN that "worked" on your split will misfire on theirs. The data is simulated with "non-linear effects and noise," which is the regime where a non-parametric method like kNN can shine — or, if you skip scaling and ignore the curse of dimensionality, quietly fail. kNN has not appeared as a stand-alone derivation question; it appears as a baseline classifier to deploy and justify.
:::

## 8. Math {#sec-knn-math}

::: {.math-section}
::: {.math-off-hint}
*Math is off. Use the **Math** toggle in the top bar to show the course-level derivation (and "full" for the rigorous version).*
:::

::: {.callout-math-a}
**Mode A — course level.** *(Throughout, $K$ is the number of neighbors; the course/sklearn write this as `k`/`n_neighbors`, and $p$ is the number of features — see the [notation table](../appendix/notation_table.qmd).)* kNN has nothing to fit; the whole method is a **distance** and a **vote**. The course defines distance as the **Euclidean** metric *(notebook `03_Supervised_learning_with_kNN (1).ipynb`, cell 3; Lecture 2, slide 8/10 names Euclidean as the metric "that matters")* — between a query $x$ and a training point $x'$ in $p$ features,
$$d(x,x') = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{p}\bigl(x_j - x'_j\bigr)^2},$$
which is exactly what the from-scratch code computes, `np.sqrt(np.sum((x - y)**2))` *(cell 7)*. Because every coordinate enters in its raw units, a feature on a larger numeric scale dominates the sum — the algebraic reason scaling is mandatory (§3, Example 3).

To predict, take the set $\mathcal{N}_K(x)$ of the $K$ training points with the smallest $d(x,x')$ (the code's `np.argsort(distances)[:K]`) and **vote**. For **classification** with classes $c$, assign the majority label,
$$\hat{y}(x) = \arg\max_{c}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}_K(x)} \mathbb{1}[\,y_i = c\,],$$
which the notebook implements as `np.bincount(...).argmax()` *(cell 7)*. For **regression** the same neighborhood is averaged, $\hat{y}(x) = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}_K(x)} y_i$ (Lecture 2, slide 8/10 — kNN does "classification (label) + regression (value)"). The sklearn default `weights='uniform'` gives every neighbor an equal vote; the **weighted-vote** variant `weights='distance'` weights neighbor $i$ by $1/d(x,x_i)$, letting closer points count more (§3).

**Reading $K$ as the bias–variance dial.** $K=1$ copies the nearest label, so the boundary chases individual points — **high variance**; large $K$ averages over a wide neighborhood and washes out local structure toward the global majority — **high bias** (Lecture 2, slide 8/10). The course's prescription is therefore to **choose $K$ by cross-validation**, never off the test set (Lecture 2, slide 8/10; Example 2). The rigorous version of "why distances stop being informative as $p$ grows," and the asymptotic optimality that justifies kNN at all, are in Mode B. Foundations: [linear-algebra essentials](../appendix/math_appendix.qmd#sec-linalg).
:::

::: {.callout-math-b}
**Mode B — full rigor.** *(Supplemental — the course slides treat kNN conceptually only, Lecture 2 slide 8/10. Anchored to ESL §13.3 "k-Nearest-Neighbor Classifiers" (printed pp. 463–468) and ESL §2.5 "Local Methods in High Dimensions" (printed pp. 22–25), with ISL §2.2.3 for the Bayes connection.)*

**The Bayes target.** kNN is best understood as an estimator of the **Bayes classifier**, the rule that minimizes test error by assigning $x_0$ to the class $j$ maximizing $\Pr(Y=j \mid X=x_0)$ (ISL eq. 2.10). Its error, the irreducible **Bayes error rate** $1 - \mathrm{E}\!\bigl[\max_j \Pr(Y=j\mid X)\bigr]$ (ISL eq. 2.11), is the floor no classifier can beat. Since the conditional distribution is unknown, kNN *estimates* it by the neighborhood frequency,
$$\Pr(Y=j \mid X=x_0) \approx \frac{1}{K}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}_0} \mathbb{1}(y_i = j) \qquad \text{(ISL eq. 2.12),}$$
then classifies to the largest. ESL writes the same memory-based rule with Euclidean distance $d_{(i)} = \lVert x_{(i)} - x_0 \rVert$ (ESL eq. 13.1), noting one "first standardize[s] each of the features to have mean zero and variance 1" (ESL §13.3) — the rigorous statement of §3's scaling rule.

**1-NN error ≤ 2× Bayes (Cover–Hart).** ESL gives the classic asymptotic bound. Let $k^\ast$ be the dominant class at $x$ and $p_k(x)$ the true conditional probability of class $k$. Then the Bayes error is $1 - p_{k^\ast}(x)$ (ESL eq. 13.2), while the asymptotic 1-nearest-neighbor error is the probability the query and its (asymptotically coincident) neighbor disagree:
$$\text{1-NN error} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} p_k(x)\,\bigl(1 - p_k(x)\bigr) \;\ge\; 1 - p_{k^\ast}(x) \qquad \text{(ESL eqs. 13.3–13.4).}$$
In the two-class case this is $2\,p_{k^\ast}(x)\bigl(1-p_{k^\ast}(x)\bigr) \le 2\bigl(1-p_{k^\ast}(x)\bigr)$ — **at most twice the Bayes rate** (Cover & Hart, 1967; ESL §13.3). The general-$K$ refinement is $\sum_k p_k(1-p_k) \le 2(1-p_{k^\ast}) - \tfrac{K}{K-1}(1-p_{k^\ast})^2$ (ESL eq. 13.5). The catch is the "kicker" ESL flags: this assumes the **bias is zero** — true only asymptotically, when the data fill the space densely enough that the nearest neighbor coincides with the query. That assumption is exactly what the curse of dimensionality destroys.

**Curse of dimensionality.** In high $p$, neighbors are not near. ESL §2.5 makes this precise: to capture a fraction $r$ of uniformly-distributed data with a hypercubical neighborhood, the expected **edge length** is
$$e_p(r) = r^{1/p},$$
so in $p=10$ dimensions, capturing just 1% of the data needs $e_{10}(0.01) = 0.63$ and 10% needs $e_{10}(0.1) = 0.80$ of the *entire range of every feature* (ESL §2.5, Fig. 2.6) — the "neighborhood" is no longer local. Equivalently, the median distance from the origin to its nearest of $N$ points is $d(p,N) = \bigl(1 - \tfrac{1}{2}^{1/N}\bigr)^{1/p}$ (ESL eq. 2.24), which grows toward the boundary as $p$ rises, and the **sampling density scales as $N^{1/p}$**, so matching a one-dimensional density of $N_1=100$ at $p=10$ would need $100^{10}$ points (ESL §2.5). ISL §3.5 confirms the practical consequence: as noise predictors are added (Fig. 3.20), KNN's test MSE degrades far faster than a parametric model's, because "spreading [the] observations over $p$ … dimensions results in a phenomenon in which a given observation has no nearby neighbors" (ISL §3.5, curse of dimensionality). This is why §2/§6 push dimension reduction ([PCA](pca.qmd)) or a feature-selecting model before kNN in wide data — and why $K$ must be tuned by [cross-validation](cv_info_criteria.qmd) (ESL Fig. 13.4 plots exactly this train/test/10-fold-CV-vs-$K$ trade-off). See the [linear-algebra appendix](../appendix/math_appendix.qmd#sec-linalg).
:::
:::
